title: Examination of Actions and Their Fruits

slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter seventeen: the examination of actions and their fruits.

slides.heading: How does an action reach its fruit?
points: An unkind word can come back months later
Intentional actions bear fruit, now and beyond
The action is over; the fruit comes later
slides.say: An unkind word spoken today can come back months later. A habit practised for years shapes a character. The Buddhist teaching of karma says more: intentional actions bear fruit, in this life and beyond it. But how does an action reach its fruit? The action is over in a moment; the fruit comes much later. Something seems to have to bridge the gap. This chapter is the longest discussion of that question in the work.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Twenty verses for two opposing schools
Then Nagarjuna replies
Karma is empty, and that is why it works
slides.say: It is also the chapter where Nagarjuna gives his opponents the most room. For twenty verses he lets two Buddhist schools explain how karma works. Only then does he reply. His answer is not that karma is false, but that agent, action and fruit are empty, and that this is exactly why they work, like a magician's creations. The chapter follows the search for a wanderer in chapter sixteen, and uses the analysis of agent and action from chapter eight.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Verses 17.1 to 20 give the schools' views
Verses 17.21 to 33 are Nagarjuna's reply
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site. Remember, as you listen, that until verse twenty-one it is mostly the opponents who are speaking.

slides.heading: Who is speaking
head: Verses
Speaker
What is said
rows: What karma is; then the problem
A continuum, like seed to fruit
Action is empty, like a magical creation
slides.say: Now the explanation. This chapter is easy to misread, because for most of it Nagarjuna is not speaking in his own voice. Verses one to five give teaching every school shared, and verse six states the problem. Verses seven to eleven are the first school, often identified with the Sautrantikas: karma works like a continuum, as a seed grows into fruit. Verses twelve to nineteen are a second school, the Sammitiyas, says Chandrakirti, with an imperishable, like a promissory note. Who speaks verse twenty is disputed. Verses twenty-one to thirty-three are Nagarjuna's reply.

slides.heading: What karma is
points: Restraint, kindness, help: the seed of good fruit
Action is intention, and what follows from it
The schools had worked out what an action is
slides.say: The chapter opens with teaching every Buddhist school shared. Restraint, kindness and help to others are the dharma, the seed of good results now and later. The Buddha defined action as intention, and as what is done after intending. Intention is mental action; what follows from it in body and speech is bodily and verbal action. Verses four and five give the Abhidharma's finer list of seven, including unseen traces left by taking or breaking a vow, and merit that keeps growing as a gift is used. The details matter less than the point. The schools had worked out, carefully, what an action is. The question is how it reaches its result.

slides.heading: The gap between action and fruit
slides.say: Verse seventeen point six states the problem sharply. A harsh word is spoken today, and its fruit comes years later. Does the action stay in existence until it ripens? Then it is permanent, a thing that lasts unchanged, which no Buddhist school could accept. Has it ceased? Then what is left to produce the fruit? A cause that no longer exists cannot do anything. If action and fruit are things with their own natures, the action must either last until the fruit, and be permanent, or end before it, and leave nothing to bring the fruit about.

slides.heading: The first answer: a continuum
slides.say: The first school answers with a familiar picture. A seed does not last until the fruit, and it does not simply vanish either. It gives rise to a sprout, the sprout to a stem, the stem to a flower, and the flower to the fruit. Without the seed, none of this happens. So the fruit is preceded by the seed, and the process is neither cut off nor permanent. Karma, they say, works the same way. An intention gives rise to a continuum of mind, a stream of mental moments, each conditioning the next. In time the stream yields the fruit. The action does not last, but it starts a stream that carries its effect forward.

slides.heading: The flaw in the seed picture
points: A seed only yields its own kind of fruit
A mind yields kind acts and angry ones
What keeps each fruit tied to its own deed?
slides.say: This is a good answer as far as it goes, and much of it survives in Nagarjuna's own view. But the second school finds a flaw, in verse seventeen point twelve. Chandrakirti spells it out. A stream of mind changes constantly, and good and bad intentions keep arising in it. A seed only ever produces its own kind of fruit, but a mental stream that produced a kind act this morning may produce an angry one this afternoon. What keeps the fruit of this morning's action tied to it, through all that change, and even across a lifetime? The seed image does not say.

slides.heading: The second answer: the imperishable
slides.say: The second school offers its own account. When an action is done, it creates something else that does not perish: the imperishable. It is like a promissory note. A loan is spent at once, but the note stays in the drawer, and when the time comes it is what makes the debt payable. In the same way the action is gone, but the imperishable remains until the fruit is paid out. The school adds details: it is itself neither good nor bad; insight on the path of seeing does not remove it, or all past karma would be wiped out at a stroke; only long cultivation removes it; and it ceases when the fruit is passed beyond, or at death. A lasting record bridges the gap. But the reply that follows goes underneath it: a record with a nature of its own would face the same dilemma as the action did.

slides.heading: Verse 17.20: a disputed summary
points: Emptiness, yet not annihilation
Samsara, yet not permanence
Chandrakirti: the second school's closing claim
slides.say: Verse seventeen point twenty then sums up: emptiness, yet not annihilation; samsara, yet not permanence; and the imperishability of action. Who says this is disputed. Chandrakirti treats it as the second school's closing claim that its theory fits the Buddha's teaching. Some modern readers hear Nagarjuna's own voice in it. On either reading, the verse sets the terms of what follows: whatever account is right must avoid both annihilation and permanence.

slides.heading: Nagarjuna's reply: action never arose
points: Both schools assume a real action that must bridge
Action has no own-nature, so it does not arise
What never arose has nothing to perish
slides.say: Nagarjuna does not choose between the two models. He goes underneath both, in verse seventeen point twenty-one. Both assume that an action arises as a real thing, and then ask how that thing bridges the gap to its fruit. But action has no own-nature, so it does not arise as such a thing. And what never arose as a thing has nothing to perish. The second school wanted an imperishable; Nagarjuna gives them one, in a sense they did not expect. Action is imperishable because it never arose with a nature of its own, not because a lasting record of it is kept somewhere.

slides.heading: If action had own-nature
slides.say: Then he shows what would happen if action did have own-nature, in verses twenty-two to twenty-five. It would be permanent, since own-nature does not change. Being permanent, it could not be made, for what is made is not permanent. Then it would be unmade, and one would meet the fruits of actions one never did. The whole point of ethical effort and the holy life would vanish. Every ordinary convention of praise and blame would collapse. And an action that had already ripened would go on ripening yet again. Own-nature would not protect karma. It would destroy it. A karma that works must be empty.

slides.heading: Afflictions, bodies, and who experiences
points: Actions spring from afflictions, which are not real in truth
The one who experiences: neither the doer nor another
No self-standing doer, action or fruit is found
slides.say: Verses twenty-six and twenty-seven follow the chain of conditions. Action springs from the afflictions: craving, anger, confusion. The afflictions are not real in truth; they too arise in dependence. How could actions born of them be more real than their source? And bodies, conditioned by action and afflictions, cannot be more real either. Who, then, experiences the fruit? A being veiled by ignorance and bound by craving. Is that one the same as the doer, or another? Neither, says verse twenty-eight. If the very same, nothing would have changed between the act and its fruit. If another, one person would pay for another's deed. The person who spoke harshly last year and the person who now lives with the result are linked as a continuity designated across changing moments: not one unchanging self, and not strangers. Verses twenty-nine and thirty close the search: no self-standing action is found, so no self-standing doer, fruit or experiencer either.

slides.heading: The magician's creations
slides.say: If that were the end, the chapter would sound like a denial of karma. It is not the end. Verses thirty-one and thirty-two give the image that carries Nagarjuna's own view. Suppose the Buddha, by his power, creates a magical person, and that magical person in turn creates another. The second figure is really created, by the first; it appears, acts and has effects. Yet neither figure has any nature of its own. So it is with a doer and the action it does. The image does not say that karma is unreal. It says that empty things really act on empty things, and that this is the only acting there is.

slides.heading: Like a mirage, like a dream
points: Afflictions, actions, bodies, doers, fruits
A mirage is seen; a dream can make one weep
Fully working, nowhere found standing alone
slides.say: The final verse, seventeen point thirty-three, lists everything the chapter has examined: afflictions, actions, bodies, doers and fruits. All are like a city in the clouds, a mirage, a dream. These images are chosen with care. A mirage is not nothing: it is seen, and travellers turn toward it. A dream can make the dreamer weep. What they lack is a nature of their own, found when looked for. That is the status of karma: fully working, and nowhere found standing by itself.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Kind acts tend toward happiness
Practice changes a person; responsibility holds
What goes: a bridge that carries the deed
slides.say: Everything that matters about karma is kept. Kind acts tend toward happiness, and cruel acts toward suffering. Practice changes a person. One is responsible for what one has done. Nagarjuna keeps all of this, and argues that only an empty karma can deliver it: a karma with its own nature could never be made, never change and never end. What goes is the need for a bridge, a lasting thing that carries the deed to its fruit. The link between action and result is real and reliable, as the link between rice seed and rice is. It is designated across the moments, not carried by something that travels through them. The books compare it to a melody known by heart: no tune is stored between playings, yet it is recognised, practised and changed.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 3, 8, 9 and 14
The Logic of Dependency: 'Continuity Without a Carrier'
Talks: Carrierless Continuity; Rebirth Video 1
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter nine, on who is responsible if no one persists; chapter three, on the rice seed and sprout; chapter fourteen, where one magically created man can stop another; and chapter eight, on Nagasena's lamp. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, describes continuity without a carrier, like a melody. There are also talks on YouTube, Carrierless Continuity, and the first of the rebirth videos. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter eighteen, the examination of the self and entities.
